claims.statement: A notification is stored as one document in the MongoDB collection named "notification".

The stored notification holds its identity and metadata at the top level and its content (parties, commodity, transport and so on) as a nested notification sub-object, beside a separate fulfilments payload.
claims.quote: Aggregate root: identity + metadata at the top, with the well-structured content held as a composed {@link Notification} sub-object (symmetric with the opaque {@link #fulfilments} payload).

claims.statement: Each stored notification has a string id as its database identity.
A notification's reference number is unique across all notifications, and the unique index is sparse, so notifications without a reference number are allowed and do not clash with each other.
claims.quote:
@Indexed(unique = true, sparse = true)
    private String referenceNumber;

claims.statement: Each notification carries a concurrencyToken that is the record's optimistic-locking version number.
Each notification carries a status, one of the NotificationStatus values.
Each notification records when it was created and when it was last updated, as instants (moments in time), stamped by the server.
claims.quote:
private Instant created;

    private Instant updated;

claims.statement: A client cannot set a notification's created or updated time: the request shape has no such fields and the server would discard them.
claims.quote: the aggregate's server-stamped {@code created}/{@code updated} instants are deliberately absent here; a client cannot set them and the server would discard them.

claims.statement: Each notification records submittedAt, the time of its most recent submission: set the first time it is submitted from DRAFT and refreshed whenever it is re-submitted from AMEND.
claims.quote: Timestamp of the most recent submission — set the first time the notification is submitted (from DRAFT) and refreshed whenever it is re-submitted from AMEND.

claims.statement: Starting an amendment or cancelling one leaves submittedAt unchanged, so it always points at the latest submission rather than the original one.
claims.quote: Left unchanged by amend and cancel-amend, so it always points at the latest submission event rather than the original one. Set by {@code submitNotification}; carried into the fulfilment-view projection.

claims.statement: A notification created through the app in a non-production environment carries an expiry time (expireAt), anchored to its created time, after which it becomes eligible for automatic expiry.
claims.quote: When this notification becomes eligible for automatic expiry, anchored to {@code created}. Set only for app-created notifications in non-prod environments

claims.statement: In production, and for notifications created before the expiry field existed, a notification has no expiry time.
claims.quote: {@code null} in prod and for notifications created before this field existed.

claims.statement: Expiry is driven by a sweep over a plain index rather than a database TTL index, so expiring a notification can also remove its accompanying documents.
claims.quote: Backed by a plain index (not a Mongo TTL index) so the expiry sweep can cascade to accompanying documents.

claims.statement: The expiry time is never shown in any JSON response.
Each notification stores a fulfilments payload (a list of documents recording obligation fulfilment) exactly as sent, byte for byte; the backend never interprets it.
claims.quote: Opaque obligation-fulfilment payload — persisted byte-faithfully; never interpreted by the backend.

claims.statement: Date-only fields such as the arrival date and the exit date accept only a plain calendar date in the form YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-07-21.
claims.quote: Makes JSON binding of every {@link LocalDate} strict, so a date-only field accepts {@code 2026-07-21} and nothing else.

claims.statement: A date-only field sent as a date-time, such as 2026-07-21T00:00:00Z or 2026-07-21T00:00:00, is rejected with a 400 rather than having its time part silently dropped.
claims.quote: Jackson's {@code LocalDateDeserializer} is lenient by default: handed {@code 2026-07-21T00:00:00Z} or {@code 2026-07-21T00:00:00} it keeps the date part and drops the rest. A caller that sends a moment where a calendar date belongs would then be told 200, and the day it meant would depend on a zone nobody stated. With leniency off the value fails to parse and the caller gets 400.

claims.statement: The strict-date rule applies to every date-only field, including any added in future, because it is set for the date type rather than field by field; timestamp fields are not affected.
claims.quote: The override is set for the type rather than with {@code @JsonFormat} on each field, so a future {@code LocalDate} field cannot forget it. {@code Instant} binding is untouched.

claims.statement: A timestamp sent where a date-only value is required, or a date-only value where a timestamp is required, is rejected with a 400 Malformed Request rather than a 500.
claims.quote: Dates make that reachable in an ordinary way: a date-only field is a {@code LocalDate} and a timestamp is an {@code Instant}, so {@code "2026-12-12T00:00:00Z"} where {@code "2026-12-12"} is required, or the reverse, lands here rather than binding.

claims.statement: Calendar dates are stored in the database as ISO-8601 strings (for example "2026-07-21"), not as database date values, so they read back as the same date on any host whatever its time zone.
claims.quote: These converters store the date as its ISO-8601 string, {@code 2026-07-21}, so no zone takes part in either direction and the value reads back as the same date on any host.

claims.statement: Storing dates as strings fixed a bug (EUDPA-282) where, under UK summer time, a calendar date was stored as the previous day.
claims.quote: under {@code Europe/London} during BST, {@code 2026-07-21} lands on {@code 2026-07-20T23:00:00Z}, a calendar day early (EUDPA-282).

claims.statement: Because stored calendar dates are YYYY-MM-DD strings, sorting and range queries on them work in date order.
claims.quote: {@code YYYY-MM-DD} strings sort in date order, so sorts and range queries on these fields work as string comparisons.

claims.statement: Moments in time (created, updated, submittedAt) are timestamps and are not stored as strings; only date-only fields are.
claims.quote: Moments use {@link java.time.Instant}, which needs no custom converter.

claims.statement: The published API schema describes arrivalDate, exitDate and dateOfIssue as format date, and created, updated and submittedAt as format date-time, wherever they appear in a request or response.
claims.quote:
"arrivalDate, date",
        "exitDate, date",
        "dateOfIssue, date",
        "created, date-time",
        "updated, date-time",
        "submittedAt, date-time"
claims.note: dateOfIssue belongs to accompanying documents (part 4); it is listed here because this test holds it to the same rule.

claims.statement: Dates and timestamps are returned as ISO-8601 strings, never as epoch numbers or [year, month, day] arrays.
claims.quote:
# Timestamps on this API are Instants and date-only fields are LocalDates. Enabling this
      # would serialise an Instant as a decimal epoch and a LocalDate as a [year, month, day]
      # array instead of ISO-8601 strings — a silent contract break. Pinned to the Spring Boot
      # default so it cannot change by accident.
      write-dates-as-timestamps: false
claims.note: application.yml is outside this part's read list; this one setting was read because it governs the date handling in scope.

claims.statement: Every notification carries a concurrency token, returned in each response, that the store uses as an optimistic-lock version: it advances on each write.
claims.note: The IT comments say a notification starts at version 0 after POST and a PUT advances it to 1.

claims.statement: A save (POST update or PUT) is checked against the concurrency token the caller sends, not the stored one: the caller's token is set on the notification before it is written, so a token older than the stored one fails the write.
A save sent with a stale concurrency token answers 409 with the code STALE_CONCURRENCY_TOKEN and the title 'Stale Concurrency Token'.
A save refused for a stale concurrency token changes nothing: the stored notification keeps the earlier write.
When two writers load the same notification and both save, the second save with the older version is rejected and the stored notification keeps the first writer's change.
Submit, amend and cancel-amend take no concurrency token from the caller, so they act on whatever version is stored when the call arrives, not the version the user last saw.
claims.note: Inferred from the signatures: only save and copy carry a token. A concurrent write between load and save would still fail the optimistic lock.

An event's aggregateId is Imports.Notification.GBN-AG. followed by the notification's reference number.

Every event has subType GBN-AG.
A notification's first event has aggregateVersion 1, and each later event for it is one higher than the highest before it.

An event's data is the GBN-AG payload built from the whole notification as it stands after the action, not the raw notification record.

An actor has the fields id, source, userType, displayName, organisationId and onBehalfOfOrganisationId, and fields with no value are left out of the published JSON.

claims.statement: Callers send the actor in the request body: inside the save body for POST and PUT /notifications, and as an optional body on copy, submit, amend, cancel-amend and soft-delete.
Each event carries the notification's full status history so far, copied from its latest earlier event.
A status change is added to the history only when the notification's status differs from the last one recorded, so repeated saves in DRAFT or AMEND add none.
Each status change records the status, when it changed (the event's time) and the actor who changed it.
The time an event was published is stored with it but left out of the published message.
A poller publishes waiting outbox events on a fixed delay of outbox.poller.interval-ms, 2000 ms by default.
The poller is on unless outbox.poller.enabled is set to false.
Only one backend instance publishes at a time: each poll takes a shared lock named outbox-poller, held for at least 1 second and at most 30 seconds.
The poller reads waiting events 10 at a time and publishes at most 500 in one run; the run limit can be set with OUTBOX_POLLER_MAX_EVENTS_PER_RUN.
A batch size or run limit of zero or less falls back to 10 and 500, and lock times left unset fall back to 1 and 30 seconds; the poll interval must be positive or the service will not start.
Events are published to one SNS topic, set by OUTBOX_SNS_TOPIC_ARN; when no topic is set, the poller publishes nothing and events stay waiting.
claims.note: OutboxConfig marks topicArn @NotBlank while application.yml defaults it to empty, so a missing value may instead stop the service from starting. The publish code is written to tolerate it.

claims.statement: The topic is an SNS FIFO topic: each message's group id is the notification's aggregateId and its deduplication id is the eventId.
Waiting events are published oldest first by write time, then by aggregateVersion, so one notification's events are delivered in order while different notifications are delivered independently.
The SNS message body is the whole event serialised as JSON.
Each SNS message carries the string attributes eventType, correlationId, schemaVersion and schemaUrl, with an empty string for any value that is missing.
Once an event is published it is marked with its publish time and is never published again by the poller.
A run keeps reading batches until no events are waiting, a publish fails, or the run limit is reached.
claims.quote:
Publishes unpublished outbox events to SNS in the order they were written, taking further
     * batches until the backlog is drained, a publish fails, or
     * {@code outbox.poller.max-events-per-run} is reached.
